Dear Secretary Reese: 
Pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 Section 35.13 of the 
Regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),2 and the 
Commission’s June 18, 2026 order directed to the California Independent System Operator 
(“CAISO”) and participating transmission owners (“PTOs”),3 Viridon Path 15 LLC (“Viridon Path 
15”)4 hereby respectfully files a revised Transmission Owner Tariff (“Path 15 TO Tariff”).  
Viridon Path 15 appreciates the Commission’s efforts to address large load 
interconnections in organized electric markets. Viridon Path 15 is pleased to present its proposed 
revisions to its Transmission Owner Tariff (“TO Tariff Revisions”) governing its interest in the 
Path 15 Upgrade Project. The TO Tariff Revisions, in concert with the tariff revisions proposed

by the CAISO and other PTOs, address the concerns identified in the Show Cause Order. 
Specifically, and as discussed in further detail later in this transmittal letter, the proposed TO Tariff 
Revisions address: (1) the application process, study procedures, and operational requirements that 
apply to Eligible Customers seeking transmission service on behalf of large loads; (2) cost-
recovery mechanisms that prevent cost-shifts to third parties; (3) the terms and conditions that 
apply for large loads co-located with generation resources; and (4) the extension of new 
transmission service to Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of large loads with flexible 
demand.5 Viridon Path 15 has generally designed the TO Tariff Revisions to be consistent with 
the tariff revisions proposed by the CAISO and other PTOs. However, given the relatively 
accelerated timeframe for developing revisions, the differing operating structures for CAISO 
PTOs, and the complex issues at hand, the TO Tariff Revisions do not perfectly align with every 
other PTO’s proposed revisions. Viridon Path 15 respectfully requests that the Commission accept 
the revised TO Tariff Revisions for filing, without a hearing or suspension, with an effective date 
of February 16, 2027.6  
I. 
BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY OF FILING 
Viridon Path 15 is a CAISO PTO and a named respondent to the Show Cause Order. 
Viridon Path 15 and its parent company, VCA, are uniquely situated amongst CAISO PTOs.  VCA 
is a Delaware limited liability company formed to develop, construct, own, and operate 
transmission facilities in CAISO. In addition to owning Viridon Path 15, VCA owns a 100% 
interest in California Grid Holdings LLC (“CalGrid”), which actively pursues competitive 
solicitations for CAISO-identified Order No. 1000 projects. To date, CalGrid has been selected as 
an Approved Project Sponsor7 to construct, own, and operate three separate Order No. 1000 
projects within the CAISO footprint.8 Because these projects remain under development, CalGrid

is a CAISO Approved Project Sponsor and will be a PTO once the projects are completed.  
However, CalGrid is not a current CAISO PTO and does not own in-service transmission facilities 
on the CAISO system. 
Viridon Path 15 is a PTO as owner of the existing Transmission Service Rights interest 
(“TSR Interest”) in the Path 15 upgrade. The Path 15 Upgrade includes critical 500 kV 
transmission infrastructure that was built as a public-private partnership to relieve bottlenecks 
along the Northern California Path 15 transmission corridor after the California Energy crisis 
(“Path 15 Upgrade”).  The Western Area Power Administration (“WAPA”) owns the physical 
transmission infrastructure constituting the Path 15 Upgrade. The entire Path 15 Upgrade—both 
WAPA’s physical infrastructure and Viridon Path 15’s TSR Interest—are under CAISO 
operational control.9 The Path 15 TO Tariff is for transmission service along this particular line 
under the TSR Interest.  
The existing Path 15 TO Tariff is limited in scope because it governs only Viridon Path 
15’s TSR Interest. Based on the unique ownership structure for the Path 15 Upgrade, Section 8 of 
the existing Path 15 TO Tariff directs requests for interconnection, construction of transmission 
expansions and facility upgrades to WAPA, Pacific Gas & Electric Company (“PG&E”), or the 
CAISO, as applicable.10  Similarly, Section 9 of the existing Path 15 TO Tariff directs expansion 
requests to WAPA, PG&E, or the CAISO.11  Notwithstanding this direction, the Path 15 TO Tariff 
includes transmission interconnection and expansion provisions in existing subsections 8a and 9a.  
These tariff subsections specifically denote that “Section 8a and Section 9a, and their subparts, are 
provided for consistency with other PTOs’ TO Tariffs. Sections 8a and 9a, and their subparts, have 
no application to the Entitlements turned over to the ISO’s operational control.”12 Viridon Path 15 
maintains this framework in the TO Tariff Revisions by incorporating new Sections 10 and 10a to

address large load interconnections.  Similar to Sections 8 and 9, new Section 10 provides that new 
interconnections to the Path 15 Upgrade must apply to WAPA, PG&E, or the CAISO, as 
applicable. New Section 10a describes a proposed interconnection process that is provided only to 
maintain consistency with other PTO tariffs.  Because Viridon Path 15 owns only the TSR Interest 
in the Path 15 Upgrade, all interconnection requests to the Path 15 Upgrade infrastructure will be 
routed to the physical asset owner. The TO Tariff Revisions are necessary because Viridon Path 
15 is a named respondent to the Show Cause Order.  
Since the Commission issued the Show Cause Order, Viridon Path 15 has worked 
collaboratively with the CAISO and other CAISO PTOs to address the issues identified in the 
Show Cause Order.13 Through that process, Viridon Path 15 developed the TO Tariff Revisions 
that it hereby submits to the Commission. The TO Tariff Revisions, together with the concurrently 
filed tariff revisions from the CAISO and other PTOs, address the issues in the Show Cause Order. 
The TO Tariff Revisions are intended to be consistent with the provisions in CAISO’s most recent 
proposed tariff revisions as reflected in its October 30th Second Revised Draft Tariff Language.14  
The TO Tariff Revisions are also intended to be consistent with other PTO tariff revisions filed in 
response to the Show Cause Order, to the extent possible. Insofar as Viridon is aware of differences 
between its TO Tariff Revisions and those expected to be proposed by other PTOs, Viridon has 
made efforts to explain the rationale for those differences.   
II. 
DESCRIPTION AND BASIS FOR THE TO TARIFF REVISIONS 
Viridon developed the TO Tariff Revisions to respond to the concerns identified in the 
Show Cause Order regarding transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads. 
As described below, the proposed revisions address application and study procedures, ongoing 
operational requirements and service agreements, cost recovery, co-located generation, and 
flexible interim interconnection service. Viridon Path 15 has sought to align these provisions with 
CAISO’s proposed tariff framework and the approaches developed with other PTOs, while 
accounting for its role as a non-load-serving PTO and the need for coordination among affected 
transmission owners. 
 
13 See, e.g., Comments of Viridon California Submitted Regarding CAISO Large Loads Straw Proposal (Submitted 
Aug. 28, 2026), https://stakeholdercenter.caiso.com/Comments/AllComments/43a11ec9-fe21-4255-bb1c-
336ad3703845#org-6c9bf931-895d-4eae-81ad-98b9e78738e0.  
14 See https://stakeholdercenter.caiso.com/InitiativeDocuments/Second-Revised-Draft-Tariff-Language-Large-
Loads-Order-to-Show-Cause-Oct-30-2026.docx (opens link) (“Second Revised Draft Tariff Language”).

Ms. Debbie-Anne A. Reese 
November 16, 2026 
Page 5 
 
 
 
As discussed below, the TO Tariff Revisions are designed to facilitate timely large load 
interconnections, protect other transmission customers from cost shifts, and maintain reliable 
transmission system operations. Further, the TO Tariff Revisions specifically address co-located 
generation and the conditions under which flexible large loads may obtain interim interconnection 
service subject to operating limits and curtailment obligations. The proposed tariff changes do not 
disrupt existing commercial agreements as there are no existing requests to use the TSR Interest 
to large loads or any other End User.15 Finally, Section II.E discusses electrically proximate 
generation and explains why, consistent with CAISO’s recommendation, Viridon Path 15 does not 
propose revisions addressing this topic at this time. 
A. 
Application and Study Procedures Applicable to Eligible Customers Seeking 
Transmission Service on Behalf of Large Loads 
The Show Cause Order identifies that the Commission is concerned that CAISO and/or 
PTOs do not currently have tariff provisions expressly addressing how the provision of 
transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads will be studied in a timely 
fashion.16 The Commission therefore directed CAISO and the PTOs “to explain whether their 
tariffs remain just and reasonable without an application process, study procedures, and ongoing 
operational requirements that address the unique characteristics and challenges of providing 
transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads, or to propose appropriate tariff 
revisions.”17 
The Commission specifically identified four particular areas in which tariff provisions 
could be improved to address the process for providing transmission service to Eligible Customers 
on behalf of large loads: (1) definition of large load; (2) the application process for requesting 
transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads and the relevant study 
procedures; (3) ongoing operational requirements for transmission customers serving large loads; 
and (4) pro forma provisions in transmission service agreements, or other applicable agreements, 
to memorialize the terms of the operational requirements.18 
CAISO addresses each of these four topics and states in its Draft Final Proposal that it 
“agrees with the Commission that additional clarity and information requirements are necessary

within the CAISO tariff, especially if interim or non-firm service is being considered to facilitate 
‘speed-to-power,’ or accelerated large load interconnections.”19 CAISO further noted, however, 
that “PTOs remain largely responsible for processing applications and studying new large loads, 
while the CAISO remains responsible for reviewing these studies and ensuring alignment with 
transmission planning activities.”20 Thus, CAISO expects “the PTOs to collectively develop their 
own consistent set of Tariff reforms to clarify their load interconnection processes and 
communications, and to align their proposals with the CAISO’s processes.”21  
Viridon Path 15 addresses how the Commission framed each issue, how CAISO proposed 
addressing these issues, and how the TO Tariff Revisions implement the CAISO proposal, where 
applicable. 
1. 
Definition of Large Load 
The Show Cause Order states that a definition of large load would be useful to develop a 
definition of large load interconnection process.22 In its Second Revised Draft Tariff Language, 
CAISO proposed to define a large load as: “An End User located at a single site behind one or 
more Points of Interconnection to the CAISO Controlled Grid, and that has a peak load of 50 MW 
or greater.”23 Viridon Path 15 agrees with this proposed definition and incorporates it directly into 
the TO Tariff Revisions.24 To Viridon Path 15’s knowledge, other PTOs may propose differing 
definitions for large load. Viridon Path 15 supports the CAISO’s proposed definition as a 
straightforward framework consistent with existing CAISO and PTO tariff provisions.   
2. 
Large Load Application  
The CAISO Draft Final Proposal “suggests that the PTOs develop consistent application 
processes, study requirements, and agreements to ensure sufficient transparency in the load 
application and study process.”25 Viridon Path 15 has worked with other PTOs to develop a 
consistent application process, and Viridon Path 15 has attempted to develop substantively

consistent application requirements. However, Viridon Path 15 underscores that, given the short 
timeframe, the complexity of issues involved, and the large number of PTOs, it was not possible 
to coordinate in perfect lockstep with all other PTOs.  
In general, the TO Tariff Revisions incorporate new provisions for large load applications 
within the existing framework for interconnection applications in existing non-load serving entity 
(“non-LSE”) PTO tariffs. The TO Tariff Revisions do not establish an entirely separate process 
for large load interconnection applications, but instead specify additional requirements for 
applications on behalf of large loads. The TO Tariff Revisions’ provisions on large load application 
process address the required contents of any such applications, the required application fee, and 
the timeframe by which the PTO determines an application is complete.26 These provisions are 
designed to collect sufficient information to move forward with a request by an Eligible Customer 
on behalf of a large load.  
Viridon highlights two specific provisions in the application process that may differ 
substantively from other CAISO PTO tariffs.  First, proposed Tariff Section 10a.4.2(vii)   requires 
“disclosure of any other interconnection requests to the ISO Controlled Grid the applicant has filed 
on behalf of the same Large Load or any of its affiliate(s).”  This section ensures full transparency 
regarding potentially duplicative requests from a single End User.  Viridon Path 15 understands 
that other PTOs will require a similar disclosure, with a more limited scope; for example, limiting 
disclosure to interconnection requests from the same large load customer that are within the 
Eligible Customer’s footprint.  Viridon Path 15 suggests that limiting the obligation to disclose a 
single large load customer’s applications within an Eligible Customer “footprint” is vague and 
potentially under-inclusive.  An applicant requesting interconnection on behalf of a large load 
customer should be obligated to disclose any interconnection requests it has filed on behalf of the 
same large load customer.27   
Second, Viridon Path 15 notes its proposed Tariff Section 10a.5 requiring a PTO 
coordination process for large load interconnections. Viridon Path 15 believes that a transparent 
and actionable PTO coordination process is vital to ensure that end use large load customers can 
exercise the most cost-effective and timely options to access the transmission system. Viridon Path 
15’s proposed Tariff Section 10a.5 requires the PTO receiving a completed large load

interconnection application to provide notice and a copy of the application to the CAISO and any 
other PTO with potentially affected transmission facilities.  In addition, this section requires the 
PTO receiving the interconnection application to coordinate with other PTOs to determine the 
most cost-effective solution to provide the requested transmission service.  
An effective PTO coordination process is essential to ensure the existing transmission 
system is utilized at maximum efficiency.  Without PTO coordination at the application stage, 
large load customers will have limited, or non-existent, insight regarding where to interconnect to 
the CAISO Controlled Grid.  Non-LSE PTOs do not have direct relationships with large load retail 
customers and, without a PTO coordination process, may not be aware of large load 
interconnection requests that are geographically or electrically proximate to their transmission 
facilities.  As a result, non-LSE PTO facilities could be underutilized by large load customers.  A 
large load interconnection process that favored connecting to load serving entity PTO facilities 
would not be just and reasonable.  The CAISO’s Order No. 1000 process has been incredibly 
successful and the majority of regional transmission projects have been awarded to non-LSE 
competitive transmission developers.  This means that non-LSE PTOs will likely own and operate 
an increasingly large portion of the CAISO transmission system in the foreseeable future.  The 
Commission should ensure the large load interconnection process allows end users to effectively 
use those new facilities.  
Viridon Path 15 recommends that all CAISO PTO tariffs include similar coordination 
language to ensure alignment. 
3. 
Large Load Study Process 
Regarding large load interconnection study processes, “CAISO [did] not propose changing 
the allocation of rights and responsibilities for studying large load interconnection requests from 
the framework in place today: the PTOs will continue to manage the bulk of the study 
responsibilities.”28  Rather, the CAISO Draft Final Proposal “encourages the PTOs to align their 
load interconnection study procedures among themselves and with the CAISO resource 
interconnection standards and [transmission planning process (“TPP”)] for enhanced clarity and 
consistency for customers.”29 CAISO also stated that it “expects the PTOs to develop consistent 
study procedures to be completed within 60 to 90 days, as required by the Commission,” and that

the study procedures should account for large loads with load flexibility.30 CAISO also “expects 
PTOs to propose enhanced alignment of their load interconnection request windows and study 
timelines with the CAISO processes.”31  
Viridon Path 15 has largely aligned its proposed study procedures with those of other 
PTOs, though it has not had prior opportunity to review other PTOs’ final proposed language.  The 
TO Tariff Revisions may differ from other PTO study processes by proposing a serial study 
process for large load interconnections rather than a cluster study process.  At this time, Viridon 
Path 15 does not believe there is a need to implement a cluster study process.   
Consistent with other PTOs, under the TO Tariff Revisions, the Transmission Owner and 
CAISO (if applicable) will determine whether a system impact study is required.32 If no such study 
is required, the TO Tariff Revisions set forth a process for expeditiously entering an 
interconnection agreement if no direct assignment facilities are required, or if direct assignment 
facilities are required, then the parties will enter a facilities study agreement and continue the 
interconnection process.33 If a system impact study is required, the TO Tariff Revisions then set 
forth the process by which such study will be completed, including the relevant timelines and 
payment for the costs of the study.34  
Viridon Path 15 highlights that its proposed Tariff Section 10a.6.4 includes a requirement 
for a PTO to share its System Impact Studies with other potentially affected PTOs, in addition to 
the applicant and the CAISO.  Viridon Path 15 recommends requiring PTOs to share System 
Impact Studies to enable affected PTOs to study and identify upgrades to downstream facilities, 
as well as the right to construct, own, and operate those upgrades.

The TO Tariff Revisions provide for the study process being completed within 60 to 90

4. 
Large Load Operational Requirements 
The Commission also identified the potential need to provide for tariff provisions 
addressing “ongoing operational requirements for transmission customers serving large loads 
necessary to ensure reliable operation of the transmission system.”36  
CAISO’s Draft Final Proposal notes in response that CAISO’s Large Load Technical 
Requirements Working Group (“LLTRWG”) has been developing requirements to address this 
issue.37 Based on the LLTRWG’s work and in coordination between CAISO and PTOs, CAISO 
proposes that its tariff will address: requirements on ramp-rates; frequency and voltage ride-
through requirements, forecasts, telemetry, and other necessary operational data; communication 
protocols for remote disconnection; and maintaining communication channels between CAISO 
and transmission customers serving large loads.38  
CAISO then proposes that the following requirements be addressed through PTO tariffs: 
required installation of phasor measurement units or other high-speed monitoring equipment, with 
cost assigned to the transmission customer; and requirements for systems that can limit large load 
withdrawals from the transmission system.39 CAISO identifies, however, that the LLTRWG 
continues to refine technical requirements, with potential changes to flow through to the CAISO 
tariff, PTO tariffs, or other mechanisms.40

The TO Tariff Revisions would require that certain of the necessary information for

5. 
Large Load Service Agreements 
The Show Cause Order also identifies the potential need for “pro forma provisions in 
transmission service agreements, or other applicable agreements, to memorialize” the terms set 
forth regarding operational requirements.42 The Commission explained its concern that “without 
such pro forma provisions in a transmission service agreement, or other applicable agreement, 
between CAISO and/or the Participating Transmission Owner and the transmission customer, 
CAISO may be unable to enforce ongoing operational requirements for transmission customers 
taking transmission service on behalf of large loads.”43  
To address this issue, CAISO proposes that the PTOs develop “consistent pro forma 
agreements to memorialize the technical and operational terms the Order describes.”44 CAISO 
explains that, in its view, “it is not clear whether the CAISO should always be a signatory to a 
three-party agreement for large load interconnections.”45 CAISO identifies that it would likely 
need to be a signatory in an agreement addressing non-firm interconnection service based on the 
operational procedures necessary to provide such service.46 And for co-located large loads with 
exporting generation, CAISO states that it would need to be a party to “a pro forma agreement that 
bridges the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (LGIA) with the pro forma 
large load interconnection agreement or negotiate a non-conforming LGIA to account for certain 
details of the co-located large load interconnection on an individual basis.”47 
The TO Tariff Revisions contemplate a Large Load Interconnection Agreement that will 
require the applicant to provide the technical and operational requirements provided by the Show

Cause Order and the CAISO’s proposed tariffs.48 Viridon Path 15 understands that CAISO PTOs 
have developed a pro forma Large Load Interconnection Agreement that incorporates these 
technical and operational requirements, but Viridon Path 15 was not able to substantively review 
the proposal prior to making this filing.  In an effort to coordinate with other PTOs and maintain

Load Interconnection Agreement proposed by other CAISO PTOs and provide recommended edits 
or comments as necessary.   
B. 
Cost-Recovery Mechanisms that Prevent Cost-Shifts to Third Parties 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily found “that cost transparency 
measures are needed to provide stakeholders with sufficient information and visibility regarding 
the network upgrades, and their associated costs, needed to accommodate transmission service to 
Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads.”49 The Commission therefore called for measures to 
increase transparency.50  
In addition to improved transparency, the Commission cited the need for development of 
a pro forma cost recovery agreement between CAISO, the applicable PTO, and the Eligible 
Customer taking transmission service on behalf of large loads.51 The Show Cause Order identifies 
a concern that speculative transmission service requests could result in cost shifting among 
transmission customers, which could result, for example, if an “Eligible Customer takes less 
transmission service than anticipated because the large load operates at a lower demand than 
anticipated or fails to materialize at all” after network upgrades are already constructed to serve 
that load.52 The Commission urged that cost recovery agreements “would help ensure that the 
Eligible Customer makes a minimum contribution to the transmission owner’s transmission 
revenue requirement commensurate with the costs incurred to provide the requested transmission 
service, including the costs of any needed network upgrades.”53 The Show Cause Order therefore 
“preliminarily find[s] that … cost recovery agreements are necessary to help ensure that the

Eligible Customer is responsible for timely paying the costs of large load-driven transmission (i.e., 
the costs incurred to provide them with the requested transmission service, including the costs of 
any needed network upgrades) ….”54 
To address the potential for cost shifts, the CAISO Draft Proposal proposes that the PTO 
tariffs address the cost allocation issues identified by the Commission.55 “CAISO believes that the 
PTOs may develop their own proposals to address any cost shifting, and that the current 
transmission revenue requirement and credit mechanisms in the TAC can accommodate those 
proposals.”56 CAISO also suggests that PTOs should account for the impact of construction 
contributions, revenues, or other cost offsets associated with network upgrade costs directly 
attributed to large loads and paid for by the large load customer through the utility distribution 
company or metered subsystem in determining its transmission revenue requirement.57  
As to cost data transparency, CAISO identifies the data already shared on its website and

Rates, Terms, and Conditions for Large Loads Co-Located with Generation 
Resources  
The Show Cause Order directed CAISO and PTOs, to the extent applicable to PTO tariffs, 
to explain whether their tariffs are “just and reasonable without provisions addressing the rates, 
terms, and conditions that apply to interconnection customers serving co-located load and for 
Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Eligible Load, or [to] propose Tariff 
revisions establishing the rates, terms, and conditions that apply to co-location arrangements.”59  
The CAISO Draft Final Proposal states in response to this concern that CAISO proposes 
to clarify co-location arrangements that would not require a CAISO resource interconnection 
request and could be accommodated through applicable PTO or CPUC-jurisdictional retail 
interconnection tariffs.60 Additionally, for large loads seeking to co-locate with new generation 
that may export to the grid, CAISO proposes requiring a CAISO interconnection study, with 
scoring and study results based on the requested capacity figures the developer may provide, 
allowing the generator to “significantly limit the generation potentially to be exported based on 
how much generation will serve the large load.”61  
Accordingly, because of the changes CAISO intends to make to address co-located loads 
set forth in its Second Revised Draft Tariff Language, PTOs do not need to make extensive 
revisions to specifically address co-located loads in their tariffs. The TO Tariff Revisions 
specifically address co-located large loads by providing that large loads with co-located generation

Behalf of Flexible Large Loads  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission identified that flexible large loads can 
potentially defer the need for transmission network upgrades, which in turn would allow for faster 
interconnection and potentially avoid the need for transmission system build-out.64 The 
Commission further noted that the CAISO tariff does not currently “include transmission services 
that reflect the use of the transmission system by Eligible Customers on behalf of flexible large 
load, on both an interim and permanent basis,” and the Commission directed CAISO to explain 
whether the Tariff remains just and reasonable without an interim or permanent non-firm network 
transmission service, or in the alternative, “explain what specific changes to its existing 
transmission service framework would effectively provide comparable transmission service 
options for flexible large loads.”65 
In the CAISO Draft Final Proposal, CAISO explains that its straw proposal created two 
new flexible interconnection service offerings, “one offered on an interim basis and one offered 
for permanent use, to shorten interconnection timelines and reduce interconnection costs, 
respectively.”66 CAISO proposed to advance the interim option at present, given time constraints 
and because the interim option is meant to shorten interconnection timeframes.67 For the interim 
approach, CAISO proposed creating a new flexible interconnection service that would allow large 
loads and co-located loads to limit their energy withdrawals or injections until their network 
upgrades are placed into service.68 The CAISO Draft Final Proposal states that “CAISO believes

Accordingly, within the TO Tariff Revisions presented here, Viridon Path 15 has

TO Tariff Revisions also address the need to ensure that there is an enforceable chain of authority 
and obligations to curtail when required so that any flexibility credited in interconnection studies 
is realized in operation. These provisions are just and reasonable because they reasonably balance 
the benefits of facilitating flexible load additions earlier and at lower cost, while at the same time 
providing the terms necessary to ensure the stability and reliability of the transmission system. 
It is important to emphasize that for the FILLI offering to function as intended, curtailment 
obligations must be enforceable and the chain of authority must be clear. Experience with existing 
reliability-based demand response arrangements suggests that voluntary curtailment commitments 
are difficult to enforce in practice. Flexible interconnection service agreements should therefore 
include clear performance obligations, verification through the telemetry and monitoring 
requirements described above, and meaningful consequences for non-performance to ensure that 
the benefits of flexibility are achieved in practice. The Path 15 Tariff Revision sections addressing 
FILLI are designed with these considerations in mind, requiring a FILLI service agreement that 
would fill in the operational details.
